name: SharePoint  Compromise Eviction
description:
This Eviction Strategy Tool template provides a practical set of preventive security actions for internet-facing Microsoft SharePoint and IIS environments. Its purpose is to reduce opportunities for initial compromise, limit the progression of an undetected threat actor, and strengthen the organization’s overall security posture through regular system hardening, access control, and monitoring. This Template is intended to be used in addition to existing security policies, vendor guidance, vulnerability management, change-management procedures, and incident-response plans.  

This template may be exported through the Eviction Strategy Tool as-is or expanded to include custom findings and countermeasures. For more information on the use of this tool for customizing eviction playbooks, see the User Guide in the upper right of this page.

Specifics and Intent of Countermeasures
=======================================

Action: Update SharePoint
What to Do: Install current SharePoint security updates and expedite critical fixes.
Why it Matters: Prevents exploitation of known vulnerabilities.

Action: Keep Windows, IIS, and .NET updated
What to Do: Install current SharePoint security updates and expedite critical fixes.
Why it Matters: Prevents exploitation of known vulnerabilities.

Action: Upgrade unsupported SharePoint
What to Do: Migrate unsupported SharePoint versions to current supported versions.
Why it Matters: Reduces long-term exposure from software that no longer receives security fixes.

Action: Remove unnecessary open ports
What to Do: Review firewall rules and close ports or services SharePoint does not require.
Why it Matters: Reduces the number of ways an attacker can reach or use the server.

Action: Review and limit unnecessary connections 
What to Do: Review connections initiated to internet-facing SharePoint servers and compare them with normal, baseline activity
Why it Matters: Can help prevent a threat actor from communicating with c2 and exfiltration of data

Action: Disable unnecessary RDP, WinRM, WMI, and SMB access
What to Do: Allow remote-management and file-sharing protocols only where there is a documented need.
Why it Matters: Reduces common paths attackers use to move through a network.

Action: Review SharePoint service accounts
What to Do: Remove unnecessary local administrator, domain administrator, or other elevated rights.
Why it Matters: Limits what an attacker can do if a service account is compromised.

Action: Disable interactive logon for service accounts
What to Do: Prevent service accounts from being used to sign in like normal users where possible.
Why it Matters: Makes stolen service-account credentials less useful.

Action: Disable unused accounts
What to Do: Remove or disable old service, administrator, vendor, and temporary accounts.
Why it Matters: Eliminates forgotten access paths.

Action: Review privileged accounts
What to Do: Confirm which users and accounts still require administrative access.
Why it Matters: Reduces unnecessary privileged access and credential exposure.

Action: Verify antivirus and EDR are running
What to Do: Confirm endpoint protection on internet facing servers is enabled, healthy, and reporting normally.
Why it Matters: Helps prevent security controls from silently failing.

Action: Verify SharePoint AMSI is enabled
What to Do: Confirm SharePoint AMSI protection remains enabled and functioning.
Why it Matters: Helps inspect and block malicious SharePoint or .NET activity.

Action: Review firewall rules 
What to Do: Remove obsolete, temporary, duplicate, or overly broad firewall rules.
Why it Matters: Prevents unnecessary network access from accumulating.

Action: Review installed software and services
What to Do: Remove unused applications, IIS components, utilities, and services.
Why it Matters: Reduces the server's overall attack surface.

Action: Restrict internet exposure
What to Do: Expose only the SharePoint or IIS services that truly need to be public.
Why it Matters: Reduces externally reachable attack surface.

Action: Back up critical configuration
What to Do: Maintain current, tested backups of important SharePoint configuration and data.
Why it Matters: Improves recovery if the system is compromised or damaged.

Action: Document expected SharePoint connections
What to Do: Keep a simple list of the DC, DNS, SQL, file servers, and other systems SharePoint is expected to contact.
Why it Matters: Makes unusual or unauthorized connections easier to identify.

Action: Review logs
What to Do: Check for unusual administrator logins, repeated failed logins, unexpected remote access, or abnormal server connections.
Why it Matters: Provides basic detection without requiring advanced monitoring.
